_Ulysses_ by James Joyce, Paris: Shakespeare, 1922

The publication history of _Ulysses_ is complex. There have been at least 18 editions, and variations among different impressions of each edition.

According to Joyce scholar Jack Dalton, the first edition of _Ulysses_ contained over 2,000 errors.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-102) As subsequent editions attempted to correct these mistakes, they would often add more, due in part to the difficulty of separating non-authorial errors from Joyce's deliberate "errors" devised to challenge the reader.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-mac-56)

Notable editions include:[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-103)

*   Paris: Shakespeare and Company, 1922: The private,[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-bbc/m001bvp2-104) first edition published in Paris on 2 February 1922 (Joyce's 40th birthday) by Sylvia Beach's [Shakespeare and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare_and_Company_(1919%E2%80%931941) "Shakespeare and Company (1919–1941)"). Beach commissioned [Maurice Darantiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Darantiere?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maurice Darantiere (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice%20Darantiere "fr:Maurice Darantiere")] in [Dijon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijon "Dijon") to print 1,000 numbered copies consisting of 100 signed copies on Dutch handmade paper (350 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc#French_franc "Franc")), 150 numbered copies on [vergé d'Arches paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arches_paper "Arches paper") (250 francs), and 750 copies on handmade paper (150 francs),[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-bbc/m001bvp2-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-105) plus an extra 20 unnumbered copies on mixed paper for libraries and press.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-The_National_Library_of_Ireland-108)
*   London: [Egoist Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Egoist_(periodical) "The Egoist (periodical)"), 1922: The first English edition published by [Harriet Shaw Weaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Shaw_Weaver "Harriet Shaw Weaver")'s Egoist Press in October 1922. For [legal reasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#Censorship) the book was printed on behalf of Egoist Press by [John Rodker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rodker "John Rodker") using the same printer, [Darantiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Darantiere?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maurice Darantiere (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice%20Darantiere "fr:Maurice Darantiere")], and plates as the first edition. This edition consisted of 2,000 numbered copies on handmade paper for sale[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-109) plus 100 unnumbered copies for press, publicity and [legal deposit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_deposit#United_Kingdom "Legal deposit") libraries.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-111)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-The_National_Library_of_Ireland-108)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-112) A seven-page [errata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errata "Errata") list compiled by Joyce, Weaver and Rodker was loosely inserted and contained 201 corrections.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-113)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-114) The [U.S. Post Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Post_Office "U.S. Post Office") reportedly burned up to 500 copies,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-115) as noted in later Shakespeare and Company editions.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-116)
*   New York: Two Worlds Publishing Company, 1929: The first U.S. edition of the novel was pirated by [Samuel Roth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Roth "Samuel Roth") without Joyce's authorisation, and first published serially in Roth's _Two Worlds Monthly_, then later in a single volume in 1929. It was designed to closely mimic the 1927 Shakespeare and Company 9th printing but many errors and corruptions occurred during reproduction.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-117)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-JJC-61) Reportedly 2,000–3,000 copies were printed but the majority were seized and destroyed by the [New York Society for the Suppression of Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Society_for_the_Suppression_of_Vice "New York Society for the Suppression of Vice") after a raid on Roth's offices on 4 October 1929[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-118)
*   Hamburg: Odyssey Press, 1932: In two volumes. The title page of this edition states "The present edition may be regarded as the definitive standard edition, as it has been specially revised, at the author's request, by [Stuart Gilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Gilbert "Stuart Gilbert")." This edition still contained errors but by its fourth revised printing (April 1939) it was considered the most accurate offering of the text and subsequently used as the basis for many later editions of the novel.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-later-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-120)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-JJC-61)
*   New York: Random House, 1934: The first authorised U.S. edition,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-121) published after the decision in _[United States v. One Book Called Ulysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United\_States\_v.\_One\_Book\_Called\_Ulysses "United States v. One Book Called Ulysses")_ finding that the book was not obscene.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-later-119) Random House's founder [Bennett Cerf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_Cerf "Bennett Cerf") chose to base this edition on a copy of the pirated Samuel Roth edition of 1929, which led it to reproduce many of that edition's errors.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-122)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-123)
*   London: Bodley Head, 1936: The first edition printed and published in England. Set from the second impression of Odyssey Press's edition and purportedly proofed by Joyce.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-124)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-later-119)
*   Bodley Head, 1960: Newly reset corrected edition based on the 1958 impression of the earlier Bodley Head edition.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-OUP22-125) The source for many later editions by other publishers.
*   Random House, 1961: Reset from the 1960 Bodley Head edition.
*   _Ulysses: A Critical and Synoptic Edition_. Garland, 1984: Edited by Hans Walter Gabler.
*   _Ulysses: A Reader's Edition_. Lilliput Press, 1997: Edited by Danis Rose.

### "Joyce Wars"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: \"Joyce Wars\"")]

Hans Walter Gabler's 1984 edition was the most sustained attempt to produce a corrected text,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] but it has received much criticism, most notably[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] from [John Kidd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kidd_(scholar) "John Kidd (scholar)"). Kidd's main theoretical criticism is of Gabler's choice of a patchwork of manuscripts as his [copy-text](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textual_criticism#Copy-text_editing "Textual criticism") (the base edition with which the editor compares each variant).[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-Kidd-126)

In June 1988, Kidd published "The Scandal of _Ulysses_" in _[The New York Review of Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Review\_of\_Books "The New York Review of Books")_,[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-Kidd-126) charging that not only did Gabler's changes overturn Joyce's last revisions, but in another 400 places Gabler failed to follow any manuscript whatever, making nonsense of his own premises. Kidd accused Gabler of unnecessarily changing Joyce's spelling, punctuation, use of accents, and all the details he claimed to have been restoring. Instead, Gabler was actually following printed editions such as that of 1932, not the manuscripts. Gabler was found to have made genuine blunders, such as his changing the name of the real-life Dubliner Harry Thrift to "Shrift" and cricketer Captain Buller to "Culler" on the basis of handwriting irregularities in the extant manuscript. (Gabler undid these "corrections" in 1986.) Kidd said that many of Gabler's errors resulted from his use of facsimiles rather than original manuscripts.

In December 1988, in "The New _Ulysses:_ The Hidden Controversy", Charles Rossman revealed that some of Gabler's own advisers felt that too many changes were being made, but that the publishers were pushing for as many alterations as possible. Then Kidd produced a 174-page critique that filled an entire issue of the _[Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papers\_of\_the\_Bibliographical\_Society\_of\_America "Papers of the Bibliographical Society of America")_, dated the same month.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-127) Kidd's James Joyce Research Center at [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") published this "Inquiry into _Ulysses_: The Corrected Text" the next year in book format and on [floppy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floppy_disk "Floppy disk").

Gabler and others, including Michael Groden, have rejected Kidd's critique. In his 1993 afterword to the Gabler edition, Groden writes that Kidd's lists of supposed errors were constructed "with so little demonstrated understanding of Gabler's theoretical assumptions and procedures... that they can point to errors or misjudgments only by accident". The scholarly community remains divided.

### Gabler edition replaced

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ulysses_(novel)&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Gabler edition replaced")]

In 1990, Gabler's US publisher, Random House, after consulting a committee of scholars,[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_(novel)#cite_note-128) replaced the Gabler edition with its 1961 version, and in the United Kingdom the Bodley Head press revived its 1960 version (upon which Random House's 1961 version is based). In both the UK and US, [Everyman's Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman's_Library "Everyman's Library") also republished the 1960 _Ulysses_. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

British academic (born 1945)

**Derek Attridge**[FBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy") (born 6 May 1945) is a South African-born British literary scholar in the field of [English literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literature "English literature"). He has made major contributions to several fields: [literary theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_theory "Literary theory"), the forms and history of poetry, Irish fiction (especially the work of James Joyce), and South African literature. His best-known book, _The Singularity of Literature_ (2004), won the European Society for the Study of English Book Award in 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-1) It has been described as "a brilliant and engaging reflection on how to think literature in terms of the singularity of its event"[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-2) and as "a deeply important book [that] offers perspectives that can help to radically reconfigure our understanding of language and literature and much else."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-3) In 2017 it was reissued in the Routledge Classics series.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-4)

Attridge is Emeritus Professor of English and Related Literature at the [University of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_York "University of York"), having retired from the university in 2016, and is a Fellow of the [British Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-5) He is the author or editor of thirty books, and has published around eighty articles in essay collections and a similar number in journals. He has held a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") and a [Leverhulme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverhulme_Trust "Leverhulme Trust") Research Professorship, and Fellowships at the [National Humanities Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Humanities_Center "National Humanities Center"), the Bogliasco Foundation, the [Camargo Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camargo_Foundation "Camargo Foundation"), the Stellenbosch Institute for Advanced Study, the [Freiburg Institute for Advanced Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiburg_Institute_for_Advanced_Studies "Freiburg Institute for Advanced Studies"), and [All Souls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Souls_College,_Oxford "All Souls College, Oxford") and [St. Catherine's Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Catherine's_College,_Oxford "St Catherine's College, Oxford"), Oxford. Among the visiting positions he has held have been professorships at the [American University of Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_University_in_Cairo "American University in Cairo"), the [University of Sassari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sassari "University of Sassari"), the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town"), [Northwestern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University "Northwestern University"), [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College"), and the [University of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"). He was the first recipient of the [Robert Fitzgerald Prosody Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fitzgerald_Prosody_Award "Robert Fitzgerald Prosody Award") in 1999.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Derek_Attridge&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

Attridge attended Scottsville Government School and Maritzburg College in Pietermaritzburg, Natal, South Africa, and received his [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") (BA) from [Natal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natal_University "Natal University") in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") before moving to the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK "UK") in 1966 to complete his [Master of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts_(Oxbridge_and_Dublin) "Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)") (MA) and [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhD "PhD") at [Clare College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_College,_Cambridge "Clare College, Cambridge"). He held a Research Lectureship at [Christ Church, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church,_Oxford "Christ Church, Oxford"), from 1971 to 1973, and then a Lectureship and Senior Lectureship at the [University of Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southampton "University of Southampton"). In 1984 he was appointed Professor in the Department of English Studies at the [University of Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde"), Glasgow, and in 1988 moved to the USA, where he joined the English Department at [Rutgers University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University"). In 1998 he took up a Leverhulme Research Professorship at the [University of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_York "University of York"), U.K., where he became Professor in 2003.

In 2015, a three-day conference to mark Attridge's 70th birthday was held at the University of York.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-7) Academics from several countries gave talks, and there were readings from leading poets ([Don Paterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Paterson "Don Paterson"), [Paul Muldoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Muldoon "Paul Muldoon"), [John Wilkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkinson_(poet) "John Wilkinson (poet)")) and novelists ([Tom McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_McCarthy_(novelist) "Tom McCarthy (novelist)"), [Emma Donoghue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Donoghue "Emma Donoghue"), [Zoë Wicomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zo%C3%AB_Wicomb "Zoë Wicomb")).

## Major books

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Derek_Attridge&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Major books")]

_Well-weighed Syllables: Elizabethan Verse in Classical Metres_ (Cambridge University Press, 1974). Based on Attridge's PhD thesis, this remains the standard study of the attempts to write English poetry in the metres of Latin verse.

_The Rhythms of English Poetry_ (Longman, 1982). A comprehensive account of the use of rhythm and meter in English poetry that pioneered an approach challenging the traditional use of Greek and Roman terminology and now frequently adopted in poetic studies. One review called it "a stimulating introduction to a promising new scansional system that overcomes many of the ubiquitous difficulties of traditional notations."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-8) It was followed by _Poetic Rhythm: An Introduction_ (Cambridge University Press, 1995, "lucid and entertaining"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-9)), _Meter and Meaning_: _An Introduction to Rhythm and Poetry_ (with Thomas Carper; Routledge, 2003), and _Moving Words: Forms of English Poetry_ (Oxford University Press, 2013), a book that _"_ should be read by all aspiring poets".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-10)

_Peculiar Language: Literature as Difference from the Renaissance to James Joyce._ (Cornell University Press and Methuen, 1988; reissued, Routledge, 2004). This book traces attempts to capture the distinctiveness of literary language across three centuries. One reviewer commented, "Attridge shows in this book (as in his earlier _Rhythms of English Poetry_) a very impressive clarity and fluency of exposition: as an elucidator of tropes he has few equals."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-11)

_Joyce Effects: On Language, Theory, and History_ (Cambridge University Press, 2000). "Derek Attridge's _Joyce Effects: On Language, Theory, and History_, gives us Joyce criticism at its self-reflexive best";[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-12) "the book stands as a paradigm for future critico-theoretical writing—for scholarship that delights as well as instructs."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-13)

_J. M. Coetzee and the Ethics of Reading: Literature in the Event_ ([University of Chicago Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Press "University of Chicago Press") and KwaZulu-Natal University Press, 2004). A study of Coetzee's works up to and including _Elizabeth Costello_. "The definitive critical work on this most haunting of contemporary novelists."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-:0-14) Further publications on South African literature include _The Cambridge History of South African Literature_ (2012), edited with David Attwell.

_The Singularity of Literature_ (Routledge, 2004, 2017). "Rarely does one encounter a book of criticism of such ambitious scope and content executed so invitingly that what is at stake in its reading is nothing short of a mandate to rethink our notions of literary production, our sense of responsible reading practices and the fundamental importance of the literary itself."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-:0-14) Supplemented by _The Work of Literature_ (Oxford University Press, 2015). Attridge's central argument is summarized as follows: "To read a work of literature responsibly is to open oneself to being transformed by that work and there are no guarantees that the transformation will be a desirable one; if there were guarantees, then the work could not be truly transformative in the first place, which is precisely why the institution of literature requires perceptive, responsible, and sincere critics and theorists – like Attridge himself."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-15) Translated into Spanish, Polish, and Chinese.

_The Experience of Poetry: From Homer’s Listeners to Shakespeare’s Readers_ (Oxford University Press, 2019). " A spectacularly rich and vast storehouse of poetic history, both convincingly homogeneous as a _longue durée_ and absorbing in its smaller diverse details."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-16)

_Forms of Modernist Fiction: Reading the Novel from James Joyce to Tom McCarthy_ Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2023. A Choice Outstanding Academic Title 2024. "This important new work by Attridge is as ambitious in depth as it is impressive in breadth. [...] For students of modernism in general and Joycean scholars in particular, this book is indispensable."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-17)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

British academic (born 1945)

**Derek Attridge**[FBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy") (born 6 May 1945) is a South African-born British literary scholar in the field of [English literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literature "English literature"). He has made major contributions to several fields: [literary theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_theory "Literary theory"), the forms and history of poetry, Irish fiction (especially the work of James Joyce), and South African literature. His best-known book, _The Singularity of Literature_ (2004), won the European Society for the Study of English Book Award in 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-1) It has been described as "a brilliant and engaging reflection on how to think literature in terms of the singularity of its event"[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-2) and as "a deeply important book [that] offers perspectives that can help to radically reconfigure our understanding of language and literature and much else."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-3) In 2017 it was reissued in the Routledge Classics series.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-4)

Attridge is Emeritus Professor of English and Related Literature at the [University of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_York "University of York"), having retired from the university in 2016, and is a Fellow of the [British Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-5) He is the author or editor of thirty books, and has published around eighty articles in essay collections and a similar number in journals. He has held a [Guggenheim Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guggenheim_Fellowship "Guggenheim Fellowship") and a [Leverhulme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leverhulme_Trust "Leverhulme Trust") Research Professorship, and Fellowships at the [National Humanities Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Humanities_Center "National Humanities Center"), the Bogliasco Foundation, the [Camargo Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camargo_Foundation "Camargo Foundation"), the Stellenbosch Institute for Advanced Study, the [Freiburg Institute for Advanced Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiburg_Institute_for_Advanced_Studies "Freiburg Institute for Advanced Studies"), and [All Souls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Souls_College,_Oxford "All Souls College, Oxford") and [St. Catherine's Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Catherine's_College,_Oxford "St Catherine's College, Oxford"), Oxford. Among the visiting positions he has held have been professorships at the [American University of Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_University_in_Cairo "American University in Cairo"), the [University of Sassari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sassari "University of Sassari"), the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town"), [Northwestern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University "Northwestern University"), [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College"), and the [University of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Queensland "University of Queensland"). He was the first recipient of the [Robert Fitzgerald Prosody Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fitzgerald_Prosody_Award "Robert Fitzgerald Prosody Award") in 1999.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Derek_Attridge&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career")]

Attridge attended Scottsville Government School and Maritzburg College in Pietermaritzburg, Natal, South Africa, and received his [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") (BA) from [Natal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natal_University "Natal University") in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") before moving to the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK "UK") in 1966 to complete his [Master of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts_(Oxbridge_and_Dublin) "Master of Arts (Oxbridge and Dublin)") (MA) and [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhD "PhD") at [Clare College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_College,_Cambridge "Clare College, Cambridge"). He held a Research Lectureship at [Christ Church, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church,_Oxford "Christ Church, Oxford"), from 1971 to 1973, and then a Lectureship and Senior Lectureship at the [University of Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southampton "University of Southampton"). In 1984 he was appointed Professor in the Department of English Studies at the [University of Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde"), Glasgow, and in 1988 moved to the USA, where he joined the English Department at [Rutgers University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University"). In 1998 he took up a Leverhulme Research Professorship at the [University of York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_York "University of York"), U.K., where he became Professor in 2003.

In 2015, a three-day conference to mark Attridge's 70th birthday was held at the University of York.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-7) Academics from several countries gave talks, and there were readings from leading poets ([Don Paterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Paterson "Don Paterson"), [Paul Muldoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Muldoon "Paul Muldoon"), [John Wilkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkinson_(poet) "John Wilkinson (poet)")) and novelists ([Tom McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_McCarthy_(novelist) "Tom McCarthy (novelist)"), [Emma Donoghue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Donoghue "Emma Donoghue"), [Zoë Wicomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zo%C3%AB_Wicomb "Zoë Wicomb")).

## Major books

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Derek_Attridge&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Major books")]

_Well-weighed Syllables: Elizabethan Verse in Classical Metres_ (Cambridge University Press, 1974). Based on Attridge's PhD thesis, this remains the standard study of the attempts to write English poetry in the metres of Latin verse.

_The Rhythms of English Poetry_ (Longman, 1982). A comprehensive account of the use of rhythm and meter in English poetry that pioneered an approach challenging the traditional use of Greek and Roman terminology and now frequently adopted in poetic studies. One review called it "a stimulating introduction to a promising new scansional system that overcomes many of the ubiquitous difficulties of traditional notations."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-8) It was followed by _Poetic Rhythm: An Introduction_ (Cambridge University Press, 1995, "lucid and entertaining"[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-9)), _Meter and Meaning_: _An Introduction to Rhythm and Poetry_ (with Thomas Carper; Routledge, 2003), and _Moving Words: Forms of English Poetry_ (Oxford University Press, 2013), a book that _"_ should be read by all aspiring poets".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-10)

_Peculiar Language: Literature as Difference from the Renaissance to James Joyce._ (Cornell University Press and Methuen, 1988; reissued, Routledge, 2004). This book traces attempts to capture the distinctiveness of literary language across three centuries. One reviewer commented, "Attridge shows in this book (as in his earlier _Rhythms of English Poetry_) a very impressive clarity and fluency of exposition: as an elucidator of tropes he has few equals."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-11)

_Joyce Effects: On Language, Theory, and History_ (Cambridge University Press, 2000). "Derek Attridge's _Joyce Effects: On Language, Theory, and History_, gives us Joyce criticism at its self-reflexive best";[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-12) "the book stands as a paradigm for future critico-theoretical writing—for scholarship that delights as well as instructs."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-13)

_J. M. Coetzee and the Ethics of Reading: Literature in the Event_ ([University of Chicago Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Press "University of Chicago Press") and KwaZulu-Natal University Press, 2004). A study of Coetzee's works up to and including _Elizabeth Costello_. "The definitive critical work on this most haunting of contemporary novelists."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-:0-14) Further publications on South African literature include _The Cambridge History of South African Literature_ (2012), edited with David Attwell.

_The Singularity of Literature_ (Routledge, 2004, 2017). "Rarely does one encounter a book of criticism of such ambitious scope and content executed so invitingly that what is at stake in its reading is nothing short of a mandate to rethink our notions of literary production, our sense of responsible reading practices and the fundamental importance of the literary itself."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-:0-14) Supplemented by _The Work of Literature_ (Oxford University Press, 2015). Attridge's central argument is summarized as follows: "To read a work of literature responsibly is to open oneself to being transformed by that work and there are no guarantees that the transformation will be a desirable one; if there were guarantees, then the work could not be truly transformative in the first place, which is precisely why the institution of literature requires perceptive, responsible, and sincere critics and theorists – like Attridge himself."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-15) Translated into Spanish, Polish, and Chinese.

_The Experience of Poetry: From Homer’s Listeners to Shakespeare’s Readers_ (Oxford University Press, 2019). " A spectacularly rich and vast storehouse of poetic history, both convincingly homogeneous as a _longue durée_ and absorbing in its smaller diverse details."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-16)

_Forms of Modernist Fiction: Reading the Novel from James Joyce to Tom McCarthy_ Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2023. A Choice Outstanding Academic Title 2024. "This important new work by Attridge is as ambitious in depth as it is impressive in breadth. [...] For students of modernism in general and Joycean scholars in particular, this book is indispensable."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Attridge#cite_note-17)
